newsitem.title: TAIWAN: YEAREND-Refinement sends Taiwan bonds to new highs.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Refinement sends Taiwan bonds to new highs.

text.p: Taiwan's bond turnover surged 33 percent in 1996, buoyed mainly by a trading system adopted in July, but officials and analysts said the huge market needs further refinements to become mature.
A sharp increase of corporate bond issuance and a state decision to set up the island's first bond rating agency were among the major developments in 1996.
Analysts expect the 1996 rally to continue in 1997.

"With expected improvement in the yield-to-maturity system and introduction of a book-entry system, the bond market's turnover should have no problem to grow another 30 percent in 1997," President Securities bond manager Vincent Lin said.
The central bank has said it would introduce in 1997 a book-entry system, which, if enforced, could help reduce delivery risks and expand market turnover, Lin said.
In July, the watchdog Securities and Exchange Commission helped establish a national yield-to-maturity matching system, now used by a score of big bond trading securities brokerages.

"The quoting system, part of the trading system, has been indeed a success, offering nationwide transparency in dealing information and convieniece in trading," Lin Ying-che, deputy chief of the commission's bond department, told Reuters.
Taiwan bond turnover first eclipsed that of stocks in 1992 and by 1995, at T$20.8 trillion (US$756 billion), was more than double the stock market's T$10.15 trillion (US$369 billion).
In the first 11 months of 1996, average monthly bond turnover was T$2.304 trillion (US$83.8 billion), up 33 percent over 1995, according to commission figures.
Officials said the system was not problem-free.
The commission's Lin said Taiwan had yet to strengthen its central storage system to a point where investors would be confident enough to store unregistered bearer bonds there.
Taxation of bond interest is also a problem.

Lin said the system is unfair because it levies individual income tax according to ownership on the day interest is paid, while assessing institutions' tax against the full duration of their ownership of a bond.
Individuals can avoid tax simply by transferring a bond on the day before interest is paid, while institutions cannot.
Because of this, Lin said, more than 90 percent of bond market turnover was conducted via repurchase agreements and very little through outright buying and selling.
"We plan to solve the problem in 1997 through an intensive discussion to be held soon," Lin said without giving details.

The securities commission has plans for one foreign firm -- probably Standard & Poor's Corp, sources say -- to set up Taiwan's first credit rating agency with a local partner in 1997 to increase bond market accountability and transparency.

A commission official who asked not to be identified said the foreign partner would be pinpointed before the February 7 lunar new year and a founders' meeting for the agency would be held in the first quarter of 1997.
The agency will rate bonds, commercial paper and financial institutions, offering reference that now is lacking.
Such developments aim to grow the corporate bond market.
Government bonds still dominate trade, but corporate bond trading has swelled since May due to disenchantment with the mercurial stock market and a growing variety of bond choices.

Corporate bond turnover was only 0.03 percent of the T$20.8 trillion in 1995 bond market turnover, but jumped 10-fold to 0.3 percent in June 1996 -- a boon for Taiwan's bond trading centre, the fledgling over-the-counter exchange.
"Companies simply cannot raise enough capital in the stock market," said OTC exchange bond manager Yang Chao-lung.
Government bond issuance began surging in 1991 when spending for the state's six-year National Development Plan led to large deficits and demand for new capital.

As of September 1996, central government bonds outstanding totalled T$846 billion (US$30.8 billion), provincial government bonds T$33.3 billion (US$1.2 billion) and municipal bonds T$18 billion (US$655 million).
At the same time, private corporate bonds outstanding had reached T$171.8 billion (US$6.25 billion), compared with state-run firms' T$24.4 billion (US$887 million).

Private firms issued bonds worth T$28.7 billion (US$1.04 billion) in June 1996 and T$32.9 billion (US$1.2 billion) in July -- almost as much as the T$38.79 billion (US$1.41 billion). issued in all of 1995.
The securities commission has allowed foreign firms to issue bonds in Taiwan, but none has done so to date.
Only one international institution, the Asian Development Bank, has issued bonds in Taiwan, which government officials hope will come to be seen as a major Asian capital market.
The ADB issued Taiwan-dollar denominated bonds to raise T$2.6 billion (US$95 million) in August 1995 and T$7 billion (US$255 million) in December 1996.
(Conversion US$1=T$27.5)
